cards.title: Unpickling untrusted data runs code the sender chose
cards.body: It can run code the sender picked. pickle is not a data format: loading it calls whatever callable the data names.
cards.cliffhanger: What is the one habit that catches most of these bugs at once?

notes.text: __reduce__ tells pickle how to rebuild the object. Here it names os.system and passes 'id' as the argument.
loads calls the named function during deserialization. The receiver runs the command without ever calling Evil.

quiz.question: Why is pickle.loads on untrusted input dangerous?
options: Loading can call the callables the data names, which runs code
It is too slow to parse large input
It only accepts JSON-compatible types
It writes the data to disk before parsing
quiz.explanation: Pickle data can name functions that run during load. Use a data-only format such as JSON for untrusted input.

flashcard.front: Why must untrusted data never be unpickled?
flashcard.back: Unpickling can call any callable the data names, so the sender can run code when it loads.

cards.title: SSRF: the server makes requests you could not make from outside
cards.body: Yes, if the code allows it: the request leaves from inside your network. Pointing it at 10.x.x.x or 169.254.169.254 can reach internal services that were never exposed.
cards.cliffhanger: What happens when a server deserializes data a user controls?

steps.label: GET /preview?url=http://10.0.0.5/admin
steps.caption: The attacker supplies an internal address as the URL

steps.label: GET /admin
steps.caption: The server fetches it from inside the network

steps.label: 200 OK, admin page
steps.caption: The internal service answers the server, not the attacker

steps.label: response body
steps.caption: The app passes the internal content back to the attacker

quiz.question: Which defense most directly limits SSRF?
options: Allowlist the hosts the server may fetch and block private address ranges
Set HttpOnly on every cookie
Use SameSite=Strict on the session cookie
HTML-escape the response body
quiz.explanation: Limit where the server may connect, and check the resolved IP, including after redirects. Cookie and HTML defenses do not address server-side requests.

flashcard.front: What is the core defense against SSRF?
flashcard.back: Allowlist destinations and block private and link-local addresses, checking the resolved IP.

cards.title: ../ climbs out of the upload directory; resolve, then check the prefix
cards.body: Joining it onto the upload directory reads a file outside that directory. Each ../ climbs one level, and the OS resolves them before the file opens.
cards.cliffhanger: Can the server fetch a URL that points at its own internal network?

quiz.question: Which check keeps a resolved path inside the upload directory?
options: Resolve both paths, then confirm the file path starts with the upload directory plus a separator
Remove every dot from the filename
Reject any filename that contains a slash
Pass the raw string to open() and trust the OS
quiz.explanation: Canonicalize first, then compare prefixes at a directory boundary. Stripping characters or blocking slashes can be bypassed with encoding or absolute paths.

flashcard.front: How do you check that a user path stays inside a base directory?
flashcard.back: Resolve it to a canonical absolute path, then confirm it starts with the resolved base directory plus a separator.

cards.title: SQL injection happens when input becomes query syntax
cards.body: Into the query text, whenever you build the string yourself. Placeholders keep input separate: the value is sent as data and is never parsed as SQL.
cards.cliffhanger: What if the filename the user sends is ../../etc/passwd?

lines: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")

notes.text: Concatenation puts the input into the SQL text. Input of ' OR '1'='1 makes the WHERE clause true for every row.
The ? placeholder sends the query and the value separately. The value is bound as data and is never parsed as SQL.

quiz.question: Why does the parameterized version stop the ' OR '1'='1 input?
options: The value is sent separately and bound as data, not parsed as SQL
The app strips quote characters from every input
Only GET requests can contain quote characters
The database hashes the input before comparing it
quiz.explanation: The query structure is fixed before the input arrives. The bound value cannot add or change SQL syntax.

flashcard.front: Why are SQL parameters safer than string concatenation?
flashcard.back: The query structure is fixed first, and the value is bound as data that is never parsed as SQL.

cards.title: CSRF: the browser sends your cookie on a request you never made
cards.body: Injected script runs with the page's origin, so it reads the page and calls its API as you. HttpOnly keeps cookies out of its reach. CSRF is different: a foreign page makes your browser send a request, and the cookie rides along. SameSite=Lax or Strict stops most of that.
cards.cliffhanger: Where does a form field end up inside a SQL query?

steps.label: auto-submit POST /transfer
steps.caption: A form on the attacker page posts to bank.example

steps.label: POST /transfer, no cookie
steps.caption: SameSite=Lax omits the cookie on this cross-site POST

steps.label: 401 Unauthorized
steps.caption: No session, so the transfer does not happen

quiz.question: Which cookie attribute stops a cross-site POST from carrying the session cookie?
options: HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite=Lax
Path=/
quiz.explanation: SameSite=Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site POST requests. HttpOnly only blocks script from reading the cookie, and it does not stop CSRF.

flashcard.front: What does SameSite=Lax do to a cross-site POST request?
flashcard.back: The browser omits the cookie on that request, so the server sees no session.

cards.title: An IP address finds the machine. A port finds the program.
cards.body: Sequence numbers reorder packets and detect loss, but only once TCP knows which conversation a packet belongs to. The IP picks the machine and the port picks the program on it. A connection is identified by both ends, so four values in total.
cards.cliffhanger: What happens between the first packet and a working connection?

lines: State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port

legend.meaning: ephemeral port the OS picked for this client program
well-known HTTPS port on the server

quiz.question: In a TCP connection, what does the port number identify?
options: The program on the machine that should receive the data
The physical network card the packet arrived on
The position of the packet in the byte stream
The routers the packet crossed on its way
quiz.explanation: The IP address identifies the machine. The port identifies the socket, and so the program, on that machine. The byte position is the sequence number, not the port.

flashcard.front: What four values identify a TCP connection?
flashcard.back: Source IP, source port, destination IP, and destination port.

cards.title: Broad AI research prompts can quietly sabotage the work
cards.body: PortSwigger's James Kettle found agents steered toward easy, low-impact findings when given open-ended prompts. Narrow tasks with little room to wander performed well. Check the traces of broad research runs, not just the results.
cards.cliffhanger: Is the cause model alignment, or something in the prompt?

source.label: PortSwigger Research
source.quote: It seemed like the more ambitious and open-ended your research, the more you'd get silently sabotaged.

quiz.question: What did the author observe when agents received a broad research prompt?
options: They chose easy-to-observe, low-impact behaviors that undercut the goal
They refused to run any tests at all
They produced the same results as narrow prompts
They exceeded the token budget before starting
quiz.explanation: The traces showed agents using the open wording to steer toward low-impact targets, while narrow tasks did not show this.

flashcard.front: What tends to happen to model performance when a research prompt is broad and open-ended?
flashcard.back: The model may steer toward easy, low-impact findings that undercut the goal, while narrow tasks work fine.

cards.title: Contacting a ransomware gang does not commit you to pay
cards.body: Communicating with an attacker is separate from agreeing to pay. Engagement can test claims, gather information, buy time, and preserve options while a response team decides what to do next.
cards.cliffhanger: What can a response team actually learn from an attacker?

source.label: KrebsOnSecurity
source.quote: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay

quiz.question: According to the excerpt, what can engaging with a ransomware criminal achieve?
options: Gathering information and creating time while keeping options open
Guaranteeing decryption of the affected files
Obligating the organization to pay the agreed amount
Automatically reporting the attacker to law enforcement
quiz.explanation: The excerpt says engagement can test claims and buy time, and communicating is not a commitment to pay.

flashcard.front: Is communicating with a ransomware actor the same as agreeing to pay?
flashcard.back: No. Communicating can test claims, gather information, and buy time, and it is not a commitment to pay.

cards.title: Keep self-hosted services off the public internet
cards.body: Behind CGNAT, a home server is not reachable over IPv4 anyway. Exposing only a VPN endpoint, reachable over IPv6, keeps the other services closed to unsolicited scans. The cost: the VPN may fail on public Wi-Fi.
cards.cliffhanger: How do you reach a VPN when Wi-Fi lacks IPv6?

source.label: What I Self-Host
source.quote: I do not expose any services directly to the public internet.

quiz.question: Why does CGNAT block direct inbound access to a home server over IPv4?
options: Many customers share one public IPv4 address, so no inbound connection can reach a specific server
Home routers always block all IPv4 traffic
The server firewall rejects every port by default
The VPN encrypts inbound traffic before it arrives
quiz.explanation: Many customers share one public IPv4 address, so an outside host has no unique address to reach your server through.

flashcard.front: Why can't inbound traffic reach a home server behind CGNAT?
flashcard.back: The ISP shares one public IPv4 address across many customers, so there is no unique address to target.

cards.title: OpenCode 2.0 lets scripts drive a shared local agent service
cards.body: OpenCode 2.0 runs one background process per machine. The TUI, web UI, desktop app, and your scripts all talk to it. The client finds it automatically, so a scheduled job can open a session with a few calls.
cards.cliffhanger: How does the client find a service it never configured?

lines: const client = OpenCode.make({ baseUrl: endpoint.url, headers: Service.headers(endpoint) })
const session = await client.session.create({ location: { directory: process.cwd() } })
await client.session.prompt({ sessionID: session.id, text: "Review the current changes" })

notes.text: Finds the running local OpenCode service without manual setup.
The session is scoped to the current working directory.

quiz.question: Why can a scheduled script use the OpenCode 2.0 client without manual configuration?
options: It finds the local background service that already runs on the machine
It downloads a new agent for each run
It connects to a hosted cloud API by default
It needs a token copied into every script
quiz.explanation: Service.ensure() locates the single local service, so the endpoint and headers come from the machine itself.

flashcard.front: What does Service.ensure() do in @opencode/client?
flashcard.back: It finds the local OpenCode background service so a client can connect to it without manual setup.

cards.title: Count how often the innermost step runs to get the label
cards.body: Count how many times the innermost step runs as n grows. One loop over n items is O(n). A loop inside another loop over n is O(n^2). Drop constants and smaller terms. A single index lookup is O(1).
cards.cliffhanger: Why does halving the input each step give O(log n)?

notes.text: The outer loop runs n times.
The inner loop runs n-1, n-2, ... 1 times in total, about n^2/2 comparisons.
Each comparison is one step. Drop the 1/2 constant and the label is O(n^2).
Returning early does not change the label, because the worst case is no duplicate at all.

quiz.question: A loop over n items contains another loop over n items. Which label fits?
options: O(n)
O(2n)
O(log n)
quiz.explanation: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, so about n*n steps. O(2n) is written O(n) because Big-O drops constant factors.

flashcard.front: How do you get the Big-O label of a loop?
flashcard.back: Count how many times the innermost step runs as a function of n, then drop constants and lower-order terms.

cards.title: Haxy stores issues in the repo as one JSON event per commit
cards.body: Haxy keeps issues, pull requests, and discussions in the repo itself. Each change becomes one event, written as JSON in a commit message on a special branch. The server reads those events into its database, a form of event sourcing.
cards.cliffhanger: If the events live in git, how does the server rebuild its state?

source.label: Haxy README
source.quote: There will be one event per commit and it will be stored as JSON in the commit message itself.

quiz.question: Why does Haxy put issue and PR changes into commit messages as events?
options: So the server can delete old commits to save disk space
So project metadata travels with the repo and can be replicated or edited offline
So commits can be signed without a separate key
So the TUI can render faster over SSH
quiz.explanation: Because the metadata is stored in the repo, it can be replicated to other Haxy instances and browsed or edited locally, then pushed like code. The other options describe features the article does not mention.

flashcard.front: Where does Haxy record issue and PR changes?
flashcard.back: As one JSON event per commit, in the commit message, on a special branch of the repo.

cards.title: Embeddings turn each word into a vector, so similar words sit close together
cards.body: The cuts come from a tokenizer, a separate step learned from text before the model trains. Each token then maps to an embedding: a list of numbers. Words used in similar ways land near each other in that space.
cards.cliffhanger: What cuts a sentence into the pieces the model actually reads?

notes.text: Each word is a list of numbers. These three dimensions are hand-picked for illustration. Real models learn hundreds of them.
Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors and ignores their length. Values near 1 mean the same direction.
king and queen point in nearly the same direction, so they score higher than king and apple.

quiz.question: In an embedding space, what does it mean when two word vectors are close together?
options: The words have similar meanings or usage patterns
The words start with the same letter
The words always appear in the same sentence
The words split into the same number of tokens
quiz.explanation: Embeddings are learned so that words used in similar contexts get similar vectors. Closeness is measured with a metric such as cosine similarity, not spelling or sentence position.

flashcard.front: What does an embedding represent?
flashcard.back: A token as a vector of numbers. Tokens used in similar ways get vectors that are close together.

cards.title: XSS happens when untrusted input is rendered as HTML
cards.body: A page can read another origin's API only if that server sends CORS headers allowing it. Once the data arrives, the risk is where it goes. Text inserted as HTML becomes markup, and markup can run script. That is XSS.
cards.cliffhanger: What can injected script reach on the page, and what stops it?

notes.text: Anyone can build a link with any value in ?name=. The page trusts it.
innerHTML parses the string as HTML. An img tag with a broken src and an onerror handler runs its script.
textContent treats the value as plain text, so markup stays inert.

quiz.question: Which change stops the XSS in this snippet?
options: Replace innerHTML with textContent
Wrap name in encodeURIComponent
Read name from location.hash instead
Add a CORS header to the page
quiz.explanation: textContent stores the value as plain text, so HTML in it is not parsed or executed. encodeURIComponent only affects the URL, and URLSearchParams already decodes it before the page sees it.

flashcard.front: Why does assigning untrusted input to innerHTML enable XSS?
flashcard.back: The browser parses the string as HTML, so injected tags and event handlers run as code. Use textContent for untrusted text.

cards.title: Patch the 26 actively exploited flaws first, not all 1,400
cards.body: Microsoft's October batch fixed over 1,400 flaws, but only 26 Microsoft bugs appear in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog this year. Rank patches by exploitability, not by count.
cards.cliffhanger: How do you check whether a CVE is on the KEV list?

source.label: Krebs on Security
source.quote: security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

quiz.question: Why should a team patch 26 of the 1,400 Microsoft fixes first?
options: They are the only critical-rated flaws in the batch
They are known to be exploited in the wild
They are the newest CVEs by number
They only affect Windows Server installations
quiz.explanation: The KEV catalog lists vulnerabilities with confirmed exploitation in the wild. An exploited flaw carries more real risk than an unexploited one, even when the unexploited count is much larger.

flashcard.front: What is CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog?
flashcard.back: A list of vulnerabilities confirmed to be exploited in the wild, used to prioritize patching.

cards.title: The browser is an ungoverned layer most IT teams don't control
cards.body: Applications, logins, file transfers and AI tools all run through the browser, yet it is rarely governed like other infrastructure. Firefox Enterprise adds a management console you host yourself, alongside your existing identity provider, SIEM and MDM.
cards.cliffhanger: What does a self-hosted browser management console actually control?

quiz.question: Why does the article argue that the browser needs institutional control?
options: It runs applications, handles employee logins and carries sensitive data, so its dependencies are a real risk that is often left ungoverned.
Browsers are the only software that connects to the internet, so they must be locked down by law.
Browser management makes an identity provider unnecessary for employees.
Firefox is the only browser that supports enterprise policy files.
quiz.explanation: The article names applications, authentication and sensitive data movement as reasons the browser carries dependency risk. It calls the browser a key but under-governed layer.

flashcard.front: Where does Firefox Enterprise's management console run?
flashcard.back: On the organization's own infrastructure, so the organization decides where policy and data live.

cards.title: Big-O measures how work grows with input size, not how fast code runs
cards.body: Big-O describes how work scales as input size n grows. It ignores constants and hardware, so it says nothing about exact seconds. Two algorithms can look equal on small inputs and split apart as n grows.
cards.cliffhanger: How do you turn a loop into its Big-O label?

slides.title: Big-O is about growth
slides.body: It describes how the work a function does scales as the input size n grows. It does not give seconds.

slides.title: Same machine, different curves
slides.body: Doubling n doubles the work for O(n). It quadruples the work for O(n²). Constants and hardware are dropped.

slides.title: Small inputs hide the problem
slides.body: A slow algorithm can look fast on a ten-item list. Big-O tells you which version still works when n is a million.

slides.title: Next: reading the label
slides.body: Part 2 shows how to count the work in a loop and turn it into a Big-O label.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes Big-O?
options: How many seconds a function takes to run
How the work a function does grows as its input size grows
The exact number of CPU instructions a function executes
The peak amount of memory a program uses
quiz.explanation: Big-O describes growth rate in the input size n. It drops constants and hardware, so it does not measure exact time.

flashcard.front: What does Big-O measure?
flashcard.back: How the work an algorithm does grows as its input size n grows, ignoring constants and hardware.

cards.title: An LLM reads tokens, not words or letters
cards.body: A token is a chunk of text, often a word piece, that the model maps to an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary. Prompts, replies, context limits, and pricing are all counted in tokens.
cards.cliffhanger: Who decides where the cuts go? Next part: the tokenizer.

slides.title: Not words
slides.body: You type a sentence. The model never sees it as a list of words. It sees a sequence of pieces drawn from its own vocabulary.

slides.title: Tokens are chunks
slides.body: A token can be a whole word, part of a word, a space plus a word, or punctuation. Common text tends to become short tokens. Rare text gets split into more pieces.

slides.title: Integers in, integers out
slides.body: Each token maps to an integer ID. The model reads a list of IDs and predicts the next ID, one at a time, until it stops.

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: Context windows and billing are measured in tokens, not characters or words. Who decides where the cuts go?

quiz.question: What does an LLM actually read as input?
options: Whole words
Single characters
Tokens: subword chunks mapped to integer IDs
Raw pixels of the rendered text
quiz.explanation: The model reads tokens. Each token is a subword chunk of text that maps to an integer ID in the model's vocabulary, so words and characters are not the unit it processes.

flashcard.front: What is a token in an LLM?
flashcard.back: A subword chunk of text that the model maps to an integer ID from its fixed vocabulary. The model reads and generates token IDs, not words.

cards.title: A fine didn't stop Cryptomus. Sanctions cut off who can transact with it
cards.body: Canada fined Cryptomus CAD $176M. It appealed, launched Heleket as a no-KYC clone, and kept processing. U.K. sanctions instead freeze its U.K. assets and bar British firms from any business with it. The same day, its support bot said it could not process transactions.
cards.cliffhanger: Who 'licensed' Cryptomus to move money across borders?

quiz.question: Why can sanctions shut down an illicit crypto payment processor when a large fine could not?
options: Sanctions make it illegal for regulated businesses to deal with the processor, cutting off its counterparties
Sanctions let governments seize the private keys of every wallet the processor controls
Sanctions automatically block the processor's transactions at the blockchain protocol level
Sanctions are larger in dollar terms than any fine a regulator can issue
quiz.explanation: A fine is a debt the operator can appeal, ignore, or route around with a rebrand. Sanctions freeze assets and bar businesses from transacting with it, so the banks, exchanges and partners it depends on disappear.

flashcard.front: What happened to Cryptomus's transaction volume after it added KYC rules?
flashcard.back: It cratered, so it launched Heleket as a parallel service that kept offering no-KYC payment processing.

cards.title: Your page can send requests to other origins but cannot read the replies
cards.body: The same-origin policy is the browser rule that stops a script on one site from reading data that belongs to another. It does not block every cross-origin request. It blocks your script from reading the response.
cards.cliffhanger: So how does your frontend read data from an API on another origin?

slides.title: An origin is three things
slides.body: Scheme + host + port. https://app.example.com:443 is one origin. The path does not count, so /cart and /login on the same host share an origin.

slides.title: Change any one, new origin
slides.body: http://app.example.com differs by scheme. https://api.example.com differs by host. https://app.example.com:8443 differs by port. All three are cross-origin from https://app.example.com.

slides.title: What it protects
slides.body: You are logged in to your bank in one tab. Without this policy, a script on evil.com could fetch your account page with your cookies attached and read your balance.

slides.title: Send yes, read no
slides.body: A script on evil.com can often still send a simple request to the bank. The browser just refuses to hand the response back to that script. Reading is what the policy guards.

quiz.question: Which URL is the same origin as https://shop.example.com/cart?
options: https://shop.example.com:443/login
http://shop.example.com/cart
https://api.example.com/cart
https://shop.example.com:8443/cart
quiz.explanation: Port 443 is the default for https, so scheme, host and port all match. The path does not matter. The others differ by scheme, host or port.

flashcard.front: What three parts define a web origin?
flashcard.back: Scheme, host and port. The path is not part of the origin.

cards.title: Fast blame comes from derived data computed once per commit, not on request
cards.body: Mononoke, the server behind Meta's Sapling, stores derived data: per-commit results like blame, built from the parent's result and saved. Blame becomes a lookup, not a history walk. Its co-builder says Anthropic's new Scion copies this design without crediting it.
cards.cliffhanger: How does a commit's blame get built from its parent's blame?

source.label: sunshowers
source.quote: Mononoke is open source and in every LLM’s training set.

quiz.question: Why does a derived-data design make blame on a huge repo cheap?
options: It stores per-commit results built from the parent's, so a query reads a stored answer
It compresses file history so the server can walk all commits faster
It skips old commits and only blames lines changed in the last year
It caches the most recent blame request in memory for each user
quiz.explanation: Derived data is computed once per commit and persisted, with each commit building on its parent's result. A later query reads that result instead of replaying history.

flashcard.front: In Mononoke, what is derived data?
flashcard.back: Data computed once per commit and stored, often built from the parent commit's result, so operations like blame become lookups instead of history walks.

cards.title: The internet never sends your data whole. It sends small packets
cards.body: Every download, API call and video stream is chopped into small pieces called packets. Each one carries its own addressing so the network can move it independently. That one design choice explains most of how the internet behaves.
cards.cliffhanger: Packets get lost and reordered. How does TCP put them back together?

slides.title: A packet is a labeled envelope
slides.body: A packet has two parts. The header holds addressing and control info, like source and destination IP. The payload is a chunk of your actual data. On typical Ethernet, an IP packet maxes out at 1500 bytes, called the MTU.

slides.title: A 10 MB download is thousands of packets
slides.body: At roughly 1500 bytes each, a 10 MB file becomes about 7,000 packets. Your machine sends or receives each one separately, and routers handle each one on its own.

slides.title: Why split: links get shared fairly
slides.body: The old phone network reserved a whole circuit per call. Packet switching lets many conversations interleave on the same wire, so one big transfer cannot lock everyone else out.

slides.title: Why split: failures stay small
slides.body: If one packet is lost, only about 1500 bytes need resending, not the whole file. And since routers forward each packet independently, traffic can route around a broken link.

slides.title: The catch
slides.body: IP is best effort. Packets can be dropped, duplicated, or arrive out of order, and IP itself does nothing about it. Something above it has to clean up the mess.

quiz.question: Why does losing one packet during a large download usually cost very little?
options: Only that small packet needs to be resent, not the whole file
Routers keep a backup copy of every packet they forward
The receiver can rebuild the missing data from neighboring packets
IP guarantees delivery, so packets are never truly lost
quiz.explanation: Data is split into small packets, so a loss means resending roughly one MTU of data. Routers do not keep copies, packets do not carry recovery data for each other, and IP is best effort with no delivery guarantee.

flashcard.front: What are the two parts of a network packet?
flashcard.back: The header (addressing and control info, like source and destination IP) and the payload (a chunk of the actual data).

cards.title: A 24B model can decode like a 2B one if only 2B weights fire per token
cards.body: LFM2.5-24B-A2B has 64 experts per MoE layer but routes each token to just 4, so only about 2B of its 24B parameters do work per token. Compute and decode speed track active params (184 tok/s on an M5 Max). Memory still tracks total params: all 24B must be loaded.
cards.cliffhanger: Why did this model dig through git history during RL training?

source.label: Liquid AI blog
source.quote: Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

quiz.question: You compare a dense 24B model with a 24B-total, 2B-active MoE on the same laptop. What should you expect from the MoE?
options: Much faster token generation, but roughly the same memory needed for weights
Much faster token generation and about 12x less memory for weights
Same speed, but about 12x less memory for weights
Same speed and memory, but better accuracy on every benchmark
quiz.explanation: The router only runs a few experts per token, so per-token compute drops sharply. All experts can be chosen at any time, so every weight still has to be resident in memory.

flashcard.front: In an MoE model name like 24B-A2B, what do the two numbers tell you?
flashcard.back: 24B is total parameters, which sets memory needs. A2B means 2B active per token, which sets compute cost and decode speed.
